House of Hanover. A German royal dynasty that ruled England and later the British Empire from seventeen-fourteen to nineteen-oh-one. Ascending to the throne after the death of Queen Anne, the last Stuart monarch, the Hanoverian dynasty brought with it a new line of succession and transformed Britain into a constitutional monarchy. The dynasty ultimately evolved into the House of Windsor through marriage and continued as the reigning family of the modern United Kingdom.

The House of Hanover inherited the English throne in seventeen-fourteen through the Act of Settlement, which ensured a Protestant succession after the English Civil War and religious turmoil. It was founded by George the First, a German prince who spoke little English and delegated much power to Parliament, strengthening constitutional governance.

The dynasty produced George the Third, the first Hanoverian king to be born in England and thoroughly English in education and sentiment. It reached its cultural and political apex under Victoria, whose long reign from eighteen-thirty-seven to nineteen-oh-one defined the Victorian era and made Britain a global superpower. Victoria maintained legitimacy through strategic marriages, marrying into various European royal houses and cementing Britain's diplomatic position. During her reign, the dynasty oversaw Britain's transformation from an island kingdom into a global maritime empire controlling vast territories across Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

In nineteen-seventeen during World War One, the dynasty officially changed its name to the House of Windsor, abandoning the German name Hanover due to wartime sentiment against Germany. The dynasty's relationship with Parliament evolved from the limited influence of early German-born kings to the constitutional monarchy model where the sovereign reigns but does not rule.
